cards.title: A gifted dressing gown led an 18th-century philosopher into deep debt
cards.body: In 1769, French philosopher Denis Diderot received an elegant scarlet dressing gown as a gift. His old, comfortable robe had blended seamlessly with his modest furniture, but the luxurious new robe made his desk, chairs, and tapestries look shabby by comparison. Driven to create harmony, he replaced them all, falling deeply into debt. Economists call this the Diderot effect: the tendency for one upgrade to trigger an endless spiral of new consumption.

sources.title: Regrets on Parting with My Old Dressing Gown

cards.title: A 17th-century Dutch bank pioneered modern finance without lending deposits
cards.body: In 1609, Amsterdam faced an influx of clipped and debased foreign coins that disrupted international trade. The city founded the Amsterdamsche Wisselbank, allowing merchants to deposit assorted coins in exchange for credit in a standardized, stable ledger currency known as bank money. By maintaining near 100% reserves for over a century and settling transactions through simple ledger transfers, the Wisselbank became Europe's financial hub and a prototype for modern central banks.

cards.title: England's first nationwide property tax was invented to bribe Viking invaders
cards.body: During the 10th and 11th centuries, Anglo-Saxon kings faced relentless Viking raids. Rather than fighting every fleet, rulers like King Æthelred raised massive sums of silver to buy peace, payments known as Danegeld. To fund these staggering bribes, the English crown developed the first regular, nationwide land tax in Western European history. Though intended as temporary emergency payments, the highly efficient tax collection machinery survived long after the Viking threat vanished.

cards.title: Assembling your own furniture tricks your brain into overvaluing it
cards.body: In 2011, behavioral researchers coined the term IKEA effect to describe a powerful cognitive bias: consumers place a disproportionately high value on products they helped create. In controlled experiments, participants who assembled simple storage boxes or folded origami cranes valued their own amateur work almost as highly as creations made by experts. Putting personal labor into a product infuses it with emotional attachment, leading buyers to believe it is inherently worth more.

sources.title: The 'IKEA Effect': When Labor Leads to Love

cards.title: A pay raise can leave you poorer if you fall for the money illusion
cards.body: Coined by economist Irving Fisher, the money illusion describes people's tendency to view wealth in nominal dollar amounts rather than real purchasing power adjusted for inflation. A worker receiving a 2% pay raise during a year with 5% inflation actually suffers a 3% pay cut. Yet psychological experiments show workers feel significantly happier with that nominal raise than with a 2% wage cut during zero inflation, despite having less actual buying power.

quizzes.question: What triggers the consumption spiral known as the Diderot effect?
options: A single new luxury purchase that makes older possessions feel inadequate
A sudden drop in the market prices of consumer electronics
Targeted digital advertisements creating artificial product scarcity
Receiving an unexpected government tax refund
quizzes.explanation: The Diderot effect occurs when acquiring a new, elevated item makes existing possessions seem inadequate, driving a cascade of matching upgrades.

quizzes.question: How did the Bank of Amsterdam ensure widespread trust in its ledger money?
options: By maintaining nearly 100% precious metal reserves behind its deposits
By issuing unbacked paper banknotes backed only by royal decree
By investing depositors' money into high-yield naval expeditions
By paying high annual interest rates on all checking accounts
quizzes.explanation: Unlike early fractional-reserve lenders, the Bank of Amsterdam maintained nearly 100% coin reserves, ensuring deposits were fully backed.

quizzes.question: Why did medieval English monarchs establish the nationwide tax known as Danegeld?
options: To raise silver tribute payments demanded by Viking raiders
To finance the construction of royal stone castles
To fund maritime trade voyages to the Mediterranean
To purchase emergency grain reserves during droughts
quizzes.explanation: Danegeld was levied across England to raise massive silver tributes to appease Viking invaders and prevent raiding.

quizzes.question: What core cognitive bias defines the 'IKEA effect'?
options: People assign higher value to products they personally assembled or built
Shoppers purchase more items when moving through maze-like retail layouts
Consumers prefer flat-pack shipping over pre-built home deliveries
Buyers assume cheaper items must have inferior materials
quizzes.explanation: The IKEA effect describes how investing personal labor into constructing an item causes people to value it much higher.

quizzes.question: What is the 'money illusion' in economic theory?
options: Judging financial well-being by nominal face value instead of inflation-adjusted purchasing power
Believing credit cards represent real cash rather than borrowed debt
Assuming central banks can print unlimited currency without consequences
Overestimating personal savings due to confusing bank statements
quizzes.explanation: The money illusion happens when people evaluate income in nominal figures rather than what that money can actually buy after inflation.

misconceptions.claim: Buying a long-desired luxury item usually satisfies a consumer's urge to upgrade.
misconceptions.explanation: The Diderot effect shows that upgrading one item often highlights the inadequacy of existing possessions, triggering a cycle of further purchases.

misconceptions.claim: England's first regular nationwide land tax was created to pay off Viking invaders.
misconceptions.explanation: Danegeld was established to raise massive silver tributes demanded by Viking armies, creating Western Europe's first regular national land tax.

misconceptions.claim: Receiving a 2% salary raise always increases your real buying power.
misconceptions.explanation: If inflation outpaces your raise (such as 5% inflation alongside a 2% raise), your real purchasing power actually declines by 3%.
